rows.searchedFor: if my PR touches a github actions workflow, does it need a special reviewer?
rows.answer:
- The handbook says great care should be taken when writing or modifying a GitHub Actions workflow, because Actions can access (and exfiltrate) secrets scoped to the repo.[1]
- Workflows are scanned with Semgrep and CodeQL for common misconfigurations.[1]
- If you need help setting up a new GitHub App, you can send a message in #team-security.[2]
- In public repos, PRs from external contributors should be reviewed thoroughly before approving workflows to run against them, since a malicious PR could otherwise steal all of the repo's secrets.[3]

rows.searchedFor: a customer runs posthog inside their browser extension and their bill is way higher than it should be, how do they fix it?
rows.answer:
The handbook's Wildfire Systems case study gives the fix for this. The core problem is that extensions lose PostHog's stored identity, so the steps focus on keeping one stable ID.

Why the bill inflates: Chrome extensions create a new runtime context when switching from idle to active, and each context re-initialized PostHog without access to prior storage.[1] Each new ID led to identify() being called repeatedly, and every identify() call refreshed feature flags.[2] Those /flags requests were billed, even when quota-limited.[3]

The fix, as the handbook recommends it:
- Persist the ID manually by using chrome.storage.local to persist a UUID.[4] Wildfire generated this ID once, then reused it across all extension contexts.[5]
- Bootstrap identity by passing the UUID during posthog.init() with bootstrap.distinctID.[6]
- Avoid repeated identify() by only calling it if the ID has changed.[7]
- Reduce /flags usage by using bootstrap.featureFlags and disabling polling if needed.[8]
- Monitor proactively with the "My PostHog Billable Usage" dashboard.[9] It showed real-time data to verify that Wildfire's fixes worked.[10]

One caveat: raising the billing limit mid-cycle did not retroactively unlock flags; only new requests after the monthly reset were allowed.[11]

rows.searchedFor: how do tickets get divvied up on the support team? does everyone work every product?
rows.answer:
Not quite. Some work is shared by everyone, and the rest is split by product group.

- All technical support engineers, regardless of SME ownership, work on analytics products, which are shared because they make up the highest proportion of tickets.[1]
- They also work on unclassified tickets, which should be updated with the correct product group where possible.[2]
- Beyond that, SMEs own specific product groups, with one person from EU and one from NA for each group to maintain timezone coverage.[3]
- The product groups are Analytics, Flags, Data, Replay, and Observability + AI & client libraries.[4]

Each SME has a Zendesk view. It contains tickets from their own product groups and the shared groups (analytics and unclassified).[5] The views also show tickets assigned to other team members, so SMEs can jump in if they know something or see someone stuck.[6]

For picking tickets from a queue:
- Avoid cherry-picking and take the ticket closest to breaching response targets.[7]
- For unassigned tickets, check whether someone else is already viewing the ticket.[8]
- Support team members, who work on tickets from multiple queues, often assign tickets to themselves. When escalating, they assign the ticket back to the team or group.[9]

The groupings are based on current ticket volumes and will be split or reorganized as products grow or new ones launch.[10]

rows.searchedFor: what's the cutoff for a new lead to get worked by sales instead of just going self-serve?
rows.answer:
The cutoff is about $20k a year. Leads below the sales assist threshold are those with less than $20K ARR.[1] If you realize a lead will be too small (<$20k) to go through the sales-led process and you can't get this information from them, you should route to self-serve.[2]

When qualifying, you consider company size, revenue, and funding to judge whether they will pay >$20k for PostHog.[3] The same threshold applies to product-led leads: if you think they have potential to end up paying more than $20k a year, you should reach out to introduce yourself and offer help.[4]

Two things can change the routing:
- If a lead is eligible for the Startup Plan, route them to the application form and disqualify them, as it's not an immediate opportunity.[5]
- You can mark a lead "Self Serve - No Interaction" when it doesn't meet the qualifications for direct engagement and the automated self serve emails would be sufficient for onboarding.[6]

rows.searchedFor: I want to interview one of our customers for a story on the website, anyone I should check with before I email them?
rows.answer:
Yes, check Vitally first. Before reaching out, search for the company in Vitally. If they already have an assigned Account Executive or CSM, give that person a heads-up, since they might already be working on something with the customer or have extra context on what to ask them about.[1]

If there's no one assigned in Vitally, you're clear to go ahead and reach out directly.[2] Some customers have a dedicated Slack channel, which is usually the fastest way to coordinate; otherwise, send an email.[3]

rows.searchedFor: how did we score on the last staff survey compared to the benchmark?
rows.answer:
They only describe how the comparison works.

- Team surveys run every 6 months using the Pulse Surveys by Deel Slack app.[1]
- The benchmark is Culture Amp's 'new tech' companies with less than 200 people. We take the average score out of 5 and multiply it by 20 to get a % number to compare with the benchmark.[2]
- A summary of the results is reported in an Issue, following a template, and the latest survey results are linked from there.[3]
